human_tolerance.notes: Uses open farmland and urban areas, lawns with shade trees in the Deep South, and is not shy about nesting near human habitations; numerical tolerance limits are authored judgements.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: Louisiana lies in the Gulf Coast wintering range; robins are modelled as conspicuous winter lawn and fruit foragers, with local activity expected to peak in winter.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: The species becomes less common as a breeder in the Deep South, but uses large shade trees on lawns; April-July follows the sourced North American breeding season.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Breeding normally lasts from April to July, with two to three broods.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: Outside the breeding season robins gather in large flocks to feed and roost communally overnight.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: Northern-breeding robins move south for the winter; the Wikipedia subspecies accounts place T. m. nigrideus wintering in the eastern United States as far south as Louisiana and Mississippi.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Wikipedia: 'normally has two to three broods per breeding season, which lasts from April to July'. The exact day boundaries are a judgement placed around that window.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Early spring nesting; 2-3 broods per season in Vermont.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: Fall migration south; some individuals overwinter in southern Vermont.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: One of the first North American birds to lay eggs; two to three broods per season, April to July.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Nest building and the last broods, in shrubs, trees and on buildings.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: Most birds depart by the end of August and return in February or March; a minority overwinter in the northern United States, including Missouri.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Breeding season runs April to July with two to three broods; among the earliest North American birds to lay eggs, starting soon after the return to the summer range.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Nest 1.5-4.5 m above ground in a dense bush or a fork between branches; clutch of three to five eggs, incubated by the female alone, hatching after 14 days; young leave the nest a further two weeks later.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: Most robins leave the northern United States by the end of August and return north in February and March.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Return north begins in February and March, exact dates varying with latitude and climate. Males defend a breeding territory and are less social during the summer.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: One of the first North American birds to lay eggs, with two to three broods per breeding season over April to July. Clutches of three to five cyan eggs are incubated by the female alone; the eggs hatch after 14 days and the chicks leave the nest a further two weeks later. A new nest is built for each brood.

phases.name: moult
phases.note: Post-breeding moult before or during the southward movement; the source does not date it explicitly, so the window is aligned to the end of the breeding season.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Regional note, a judgement rather than a cited statement: most of the species winters south of Canada, but the source says that robins 'occasionally overwinter in the northern part of the United States and southern Canada', and the Great Lakes and Appalachian highlands in the northern US are within that band, so this locale is treated as holding robins year-round.

vocalizations.description: Complex, almost continuous cheery carol of repeated discrete units, often delivered from a high tree perch from late winter through summer.
Scold and alarm calls used when a ground predator approaches or a nest or robin is directly threatened, often before flying to cover or a perch.
A number of calls carrying specific information, used when a ground predator approaches and when a nest or another robin is directly threatened; robins also band together to drive a predator off.
Short, quiet 'chip' contact call given by foraging or resting robins.
A soft 'chup' or low 'tut-tut' contact call exchanged between a pair and between flock members on the winter ground.

taxonomy.note: Linnaeus 1766, Turdus migratorius; family Turdidae per the GBIF backbone and ITIS TSN 179759.

external.note: GBIF and iNaturalist identifiers were confirmed against their APIs; Wikidata properties provide NCBI taxon id, eBird species code, iNaturalist taxon id and GBIF taxon id; ITIS TSN from the ITIS JSON service.

common_names.note: English from Wikidata; the French and German names from the GBIF Vernacular Name Service, which lists 'Merle d'Amérique' (ITIS) and 'Amschel' (Catalogue of Life).

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 and Wikipedia conservation-status box report least concern.

range.note: Country list derived from the described North American breeding/wintering range: Alaska and Canada south through the United States to Mexico; Köppen classes broadly map that range and include Shreveport's Cfa.

traits.limb_count.note: Biped: two legs, the forelimbs modified as wings.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Forages with short hops/running stops on lawns and uses powered flight.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Endotherm: a bird, 'active mostly during the day'.

traits.skin.note: Feathers: plumage described in detail in the Description section.

traits.flight.note: Powered flight: a migratory bird commuting between summer and winter ranges.

traits.metamorphosis.note: None: the young hatch as chicks, 'paler in color than adult males', with no metamorphic stage.

traits.nest_type.note: Nest is a mud-lined open cup of coarse grass, twigs, paper and feathers.

traits.perching.note: Perches to sing: 'It usually sings from a high perch in a tree.'

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.077 kg, above Tiny and below 1 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: Wikipedia gives average mass about 77 g.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Wikipedia gives females 59-91 g and males 72-94 g; combined adult range recorded.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Wikipedia states the average lifespan is about two years.

traits.diet.note: Wikipedia gives about 40 percent small invertebrates and 60 percent wild/cultivated fruits and berries.

traits.social.note: Active mostly during the day, assembles in large flocks at night in winter, and males defend breeding territories in summer; modelled as flock-capable with solitary/pair lower bound.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Wikipedia states the species is active mostly during the day.

traits.defense.note: Threat response modelled as flee to cover/perch; Wikipedia documents predator vigilance, alarm calls and mobbing/defense near nests.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: common around lawns and human habitations, but still alarms and flees from direct threats.

habitat.use.note: Ground foraging on lawns/soil plus tree/shrub nesting, perching and roosting mapped to 60 percent ground, 35 percent arboreal and 5 percent aerial movement.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Winter night roosts in secluded swamps or dense vegetation mapped to shrub_thicket.

habitat.resources.note: Invertebrate, fruit and berry resources follow the sourced diet; nest_cup, perch, shrub_thicket and water are simulator resource mappings from sourced nest, tree-perch/roost and lawn/sprinkler use.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Uses open farmland and urban areas, large shade trees on lawns in the Deep South, and nests close to human habitations; urban_affinity/uses_gardens follow those statements, while light_max, flight_distance_m and road_mortality are judgement.

seasonal.strategy.note: Wikipedia describes migration from breeding to wintering range, with some birds overwintering north and Gulf Coast/Mexico wintering.

seasonal.winter_fraction.note: Judgement for partial migration: many birds winter south of Canada while some overwinter farther north; exact continent-wide staying fraction is not given by the open source.

seasonal.phases.note: Gulf Coast wintering, winter flocking, Deep South breeding rarity and April-July breeding are sourced; US-LA phase fractions and exact month-day boundaries are judgement for the Shreveport locale.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg, juvenile and adult stages are standard; 14 days to hatch, about two weeks to leave nest and about two more weeks to sustained flight give a 42-day juvenile model window; scale is judgement.

vocalizations.song.note: Complex cheery carol, late February/early March to late July/early August with some September, often first at dawn and last in evening from a high tree perch.

vocalizations.alarm.note: Wikipedia describes calls used for ground predators and direct nest/robin threats; the public-domain Commons recording is labelled with scold and alarm calls.

look.note: Brown back, reddish-orange breast, white throat/belly/eye arcs, darker head and yellow bill follow the text and licensed image; exact block proportions, colours and poses are judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: invertebrate food tag follows the earthworm/insect foraging diet, nest months follow April-July breeding, song/alarm params match local call_ids, and flee/song-cooldown values are judgement.

vocalizations.note: Song description, its dawn timing and its February-to-August season are from the Vocalization section. The alarm entry records only what Wikipedia supports, that an alarm call and a separate scold call exist; the cooldown is authored judgement.

traits.senses.note: Wikipedia states the species uses 'auditory, visual, olfactory and possibly vibrotactile cues to find prey, but vision is the predominant mode', and that experiments show it finds earthworms underground by listening alone. Olfaction is set to Med and hearing to High on that basis; no open source quantifies either, and vision_colour is omitted rather than guessed.

habitat.density_per_ha.note: Judgement: Wikipedia's statement that this is 'the most abundant landbird in North America (with 370 million individuals)' fixes the order of magnitude for a continent-wide species; typical 1.7 per hectare follows from a typical breed-bird territory of roughly 0.6 ha, and min and max are an authored tenfold band either side, following the same convention used for sciurus-carolinensis and vulpes-vulpes.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis, perching) and locomotion modes. The species 'forage[s] primarily on the ground', 'frequently seen running across lawns' and 'take[s] several short hops', with powered flight between winter roosts and the breeding range; The source describes the robin running and stopping across lawns as a distinguishing characteristic, but the biped_winged body plan has no run animation, so Walk and Hop carry ground foraging. Individual numeric and behavioural traits below carry their own entries.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Invertebrate, fruit and berry tags come from the Diet section; nest_cup from the Breeding section (nest in a dense bush or tree fork) and perch from singing 'from a high perch in a tree'. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.
